content: The text provided is a long list of references and data points related to gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), its diagnosis, treatment, and associated outcomes. 1. A 2011 study published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (Volume 64, Issue 4, Pages 383-394) discusses the importance of summary findings tables in clinical research. 2. Wendland et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review comparing the diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) established by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Association of Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG). The findings, published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth (Volume 12, Article 23), highlight the impact of these criteria on pregnancy outcomes. 3. Horvath et al. (2010) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of treatment in women with GDM. Their results, published in the British Medical Journal (Volume 340, Article c1395), emphasize the benefits of managing GDM to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. 4. Alwan, Tuffnell, and West (2009) reviewed treatments for GDM in a Cochrane systematic review (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Issue 3, Article CD003395), providing evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice. 5. Falavigna et al. (2012) assessed the effectiveness of GDM treatment in a systematic review with a quality-of-evidence assessment. Their findings were published in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice. 6. The WHO's 2008-2013 Action Plan for the Global Strategy for the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases outlines strategies to address diabetes and other chronic conditions, emphasizing the importance of early detection and management. 7. O'Sullivan and Mahan (1964) established criteria for the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) in pregnancy, which became a foundational diagnostic tool for GDM (Diabetes, Volume 13, Pages 278-285). 8. O'Sullivan et al. (1966) explored the management of potential diabetes during pregnancy and its implications for maternal and fetal health (Obstetrics & Gynecology, Volume 27, Pages 683-689). 9. O'Sullivan et al. (1973) investigated the relationship between GDM and perinatal mortality rates, publishing their findings in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology (Volume 116, Issue 7, Pages 901-904). 10. The National Diabetes Data Group (1979) provided a comprehensive definition, diagnosis, and classification of diabetes mellitus and glucose intolerance, which has informed clinical guidelines (Diabetes, Volume 28, Pages 1039-1057). 11. The WHO Expert Committee on Diabetes Mellitus released its second report in 1980, detailing recommendations for the diagnosis and management of diabetes (Technical Report Series 646, Geneva: WHO). 12. The Hyperglycemia and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes (HAPO) Study Cooperative Research Group (2008) demonstrated the association between maternal hyperglycemia and adverse pregnancy outcomes in the New England Journal of Medicine (Volume 358, Issue 19, Pages 1991-2002). 13. The International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) Consensus Panel (2010) published recommendations for the diagnosis and classification of hyperglycemia in pregnancy in Diabetes Care (Volume 33, Issue 3, Pages 676-682). 14. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (2011) issued Committee Opinion No. 504 on screening and diagnosis of GDM, emphasizing the importance of early detection (Obstetrics & Gynecology, Volume 118, Pages 751-753). 15. The Canadian Diabetes Association's 2008 Clinical Practice Guidelines provided evidence-based recommendations for the prevention and management of diabetes in Canada (Canadian Journal of Diabetes, Volume 32, Supplement 1). 16. Sacks et al. (1995) proposed universal criteria for GDM diagnosis using the 75-gram OGTT, highlighting its predictive value for adverse pregnancy outcomes (American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Volume 172, Issue 2, Pages 607-614). 17. Schmidt et al. (2001) examined the relationship between GDM diagnosed with a 2-hour 75-gram OGTT and adverse pregnancy outcomes, publishing their findings in Diabetes Care (Volume 24, Issue 7, Pages 1151-1155). 18. Moses and Calvert (1995) explored the continuum of risk associated with maternal glucose levels in pregnancies without GDM, emphasizing the importance of glucose monitoring (Diabetes Care, Volume 18, Issue 12, Pages 1527-1533). 19. Schunemann et al. (2011) discussed the GRADE approach and Bradford Hill's criteria for causation in evaluating evidence quality in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health (Volume 65, Issue 5, Pages 392-395). 20. Aberg et al. (2001) conducted a population-based study in southern Sweden, linking impaired glucose tolerance to adverse pregnancy outcomes (American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Volume 184, Issue 2, Pages 77-83). 21. Black et al. (2010) analyzed clinical outcomes of pregnancies complicated by mild GDM, showing variations based on abnormal OGTT values (Diabetes Care, Volume 33, Issue 12, Pages 2524-2530). 22. Riskin-Masiah et al. (2010) identified first-trimester fasting hyperglycemia as a predictor for GDM development, emphasizing the need for early screening (European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, Volume 152, Issue 2, Pages 163-167). 23. Balaji et al. (2011) highlighted the inadequacy of fasting plasma glucose alone to diagnose GDM in Asian Indian women, advocating for comprehensive testing (Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice, Volume 94, Issue 1, Pages e21-e23). 24. NICE Guideline 63 (2008) provided detailed recommendations for managing diabetes and its complications during pregnancy, from pre-conception to the postnatal period. 25. Falavigna et al. (2013) conducted a simulation study to evaluate the impact of GDM screening strategies on perinatal outcomes, emphasizing the importance of tailored approaches (Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice). 26. Bellamy et al. (2007) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis linking pre-eclampsia to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer later in life (British Medical Journal, Volume 335, Issue 7627, Page 974). 27. Barker (2006) reviewed the long-term consequences of fetal growth restriction, highlighting its impact on adult health outcomes (Clinical Obstetrics & Gynecology, Volume 49, Issue 2, Pages 270-283). 28. Feig et al. (1998) surveyed women three to five years after a GDM diagnosis, assessing their self-perceived health status compared to matched controls (American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Volume 178, Issue 2, Pages 386-393). 29. Rumbold and Crowther (2002) explored women's experiences with GDM screening, emphasizing the psychological and emotional impact (Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Volume 42, Issue 2, Pages 131-137). 30. Mills et al. (1998) demonstrated a physiological reduction in fasting plasma glucose concentration during the first trimester of normal pregnancy, providing insights into early glucose metabolism changes (Metabolism, Volume 47, Issue 9, Pages 1140-1144).
